issues.legal_issue: The constitutional protection for acquisition or modification of estate rights applies only when the measure is connected with agrarian reform.
material_facts: The challenged law authorized acquisition of land for housing schemes, including schemes that could extend beyond slum clearance to other housing objectives.
The acquisitions were not connected with agrarian reform.
issues.conclusion: The law was not protected by the constitutional provision concerning estates because its acquisitions were not connected with agrarian reform.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31-A applies to a law acquiring an estate or rights in an estate, or extinguishing or modifying such rights, only when the measure is connected with agrarian reform. That restriction remains applicable after the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964. Article 31-A is a limited exception to the protections applicable to acquisition under Article 31(2) and (2A), not a general protection for State acquisitions. The Court followed K. K. Kochuni v. State of Madras, [1960] 3 S.C.R. 887, and Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, [1965] 1 S.C.R. 82.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenged the constitutional validity of a law authorizing the State to acquire property.
predicates.acquisition_for_housing: The State sought to acquire property for a housing scheme.
predicates.acquisition_not_connected_to_agrarian_re: The acquisition was not connected with agrarian reform.

issues.definition: When a person challenges an acquisition law and the State seeks property for housing unrelated to agrarian reform, the law is not protected by the agrarian-reform exception.

issues.legal_issue: A law governing compulsory acquisition must provide for compensation representing a just equivalent, but courts cannot review the adequacy of the compensation or the principles used merely because another method would yield more; they may review illusory compensation or principles unrelated to the property or its value near the time of acquisition.
material_facts: The challenged law set compensation by the lower of the market value at notification or the average market value during the preceding five years.
It reduced the solatium compared with the principal acquisition law and excluded additional value attributable to the land's suitability for a different use.

The Court considered the valuation method sufficiently related to the land and its value at or about the time of acquisition, and treated the disputed exclusions and reduced solatium as matters of adequacy rather than fraud on power.
issues.conclusion: The challenged compensation provisions did not violate Article 31(2), because they prescribed valuation principles and did not provide illusory compensation or principles unrelated to the property or its value near the time of acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as amended by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, requires a law authorizing acquisition to provide compensation or specify principles for determining it. Compensation means a just equivalent, but the adequacy of the compensation and the choice between relevant valuation methods are not justiciable. A court may review whether compensation is illusory or whether the stated principles are irrelevant to the property or its value at or about the time of acquisition; such defects may amount to a fraud on legislative power. The Court followed State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bela Banerjee, [1954] S.C.R. 558, and State of Madras v. Namasivaya Mudaliar, [1964] 6 S.C.R. 936, and referred to Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 1, and Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v. A.P. State Road Transport Corporation, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 319, on colourable legislation and fraud on power.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenged the constitutional validity of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition.
predicates.compensation_principles_related_to_prope: The law's compensation principles take account of the kind of property acquired.
predicates.compensation_principles_related_to_value: The law's compensation principles relate to the property's value at or about the time it is acquired.
predicates.compensation_illusory: The law provides compensation that is merely nominal or illusory.

issues.definition: If an acquisition law is challenged, its compensation principles relate to the property and its value near acquisition, and the compensation is not illusory, the law is not invalid for failure to provide compensation.

issues.legal_issue: Different compensation treatment for land acquired for housing schemes and land acquired for other public purposes violates equality when the distinction has no rational relation to the legislative objective.
material_facts: Owners whose land was acquired for housing schemes received less than owners whose same or similar land was acquired for another public purpose under the principal law.
The challenged law extended to housing schemes with varied objectives, not only slum clearance, and allowed acquisition for housing prosperous sections as well as poorer sections.
The differences between the affected owners and lands, including extent, quality, suitability, and ownership, had no reasonable relation to the law's objective.
issues.conclusion: The challenged law violated Article 14 because the different treatment of owners whose land was acquired for housing schemes was not supported by a reasonable classification, and the law was void.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits legislative classification only where it is founded on an intelligible differentia distinguishing those included from those excluded and that differentia has a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved. The Court applied these two tests to the distinction between acquisitions for housing schemes and acquisitions for other public purposes.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenged the constitutional validity of a law authorizing the State to acquire property.
predicates.housing_acquisition_receives_lower_compe: Owners whose property is acquired for housing receive less compensation than owners whose same or similar property is acquired for another public purpose.
predicates.housing_law_covers_varied_objectives: The law permits acquisitions for housing objectives extending beyond a narrowly identified social need.
predicates.no_rational_basis_for_different_treatmen: The differences between the affected owners or properties have no rational relation to the law's objective.

issues.definition: When a challenged acquisition law gives lower compensation for housing acquisitions, covers varied housing objectives, and lacks a rational basis for that difference, it violates equality.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition alleged to be a device for raising State revenue is not established as such when the evidence supports a genuine housing-development scheme and the allegation is unsupported.
material_facts: The owners alleged that land was acquired cheaply and later sold at higher prices to generate State revenue.
The State denied that the acquisitions were intended to fill its coffers and stated that the schemes operated on a no-profit-no-loss basis.
The record described composite housing colonies with housing for different income groups and community facilities, and the owners did not deny the State's account of the schemes.
The Court found that the owners had not established that their land was being acquired as a revenue-raising device.
issues.conclusion: The owners failed to establish that the acquisitions were a device to improve State revenue, and the Court found that the land was being acquired bona fide for housing development.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the claim of a colourable or revenue-raising purpose against the evidence concerning the acquisition schemes. It explained the general doctrine of colourable legislation by reference to Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa, [1954] S.C.R. 1, and Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v. A.P. State Road Transport Corporation, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 319: the question is whether the legislature has exceeded its power in substance, and legislative motive alone is not the test. On the facts, the record supported genuine housing development rather than the alleged revenue device.

predicates.challenge_alleges_acquisition_is_revenue: A property owner alleges that an acquisition is a device to raise revenue for the State.
predicates.state_denies_revenue_purpose: The State denies that raising revenue is the purpose of the acquisition.
predicates.record_supports_genuine_housing_developm: The record describes a genuine housing-development scheme and associated community facilities.
predicates.allegation_lacks_support: The property owner does not substantiate the allegation with evidence sufficient to displace the State's account.

issues.definition: When an owner alleges a revenue-raising device, the State denies that purpose, the record supports genuine housing development, and the allegation lacks support, the revenue device is not established.
